_about: Weekly practice exercises. The Weekly Practice page picks three each week from the phases you've reached. Never rename or reuse an id: it's how 'done' is remembered. Text fields allow …, , .

exercises.title: Hello World from an empty folder
exercises.what: Make a brand new folder. Write hello.c and build.bat without looking at your old ones.
steps: Open the Developer Command Prompt and cd into the new folder.
Write both files from memory, including /W4 /WX in the build line.
Build and run. Only then open your old files and compare.
exercises.done: It builds with zero warnings and you only looked things up after it worked.

exercises.title: Escape sequence prediction sheet
exercises.what: Write five printf lines that mix \n, \r, \t, \\ and %%.
steps: Before you build, write down exactly what each line will print, spaces included.
Build and run.
For every line you got wrong, write one sentence on why.
exercises.done: You can explain every difference between your guess and the real output.

exercises.title: Five one-character mistakes
exercises.what: Take a working program and break it five different ways, one at a time: delete a ;, misspell printf, delete the #include, drop a closing quote, delete a closing brace.
steps: Before each build, guess: error or warning? Which line will it point at?
Build, read the message top to bottom, and write down the code (C2143, C4013…).
Fix it and confirm it builds clean before the next break.
exercises.done: You have a list of five error codes with what each one means in your own words.

exercises.title: Comment every line of build.bat
exercises.what: Open build.bat and add a rem comment above every line saying what it does.
steps: Include what each compiler flag does.
Explain what %ERRORLEVEL% holds after a failed build.
Run it once to make sure your comments didn't break anything.
exercises.done: Someone who has never seen the file could follow it from your comments.

exercises.title: Kill the Session 1 warnings
exercises.what: Session 1 left C4244 and C4305 in the build. Turn on /WX so they become errors, then fix them properly.
steps: Build and read both warnings.
Fix the float to int conversion on purpose, with a cast, and the double literal with an f.
Write a comment above each fix saying what was lost before.
exercises.done: The Session 1 file builds clean with /W4 /WX.

exercises.title: Guessing game in 20 minutes
exercises.what: Rebuild the number guessing game from a blank file with a 20-minute timer running.
steps: srand once, pick 1–100, loop until correct, print higher/lower.
When the timer ends, stop, even if it's not done.
Diff it against your original. Write down the one thing you forgot.
exercises.done: It runs, and you know which part didn't come back from memory.

exercises.title: Integer division prediction sheet
exercises.what: Print these with the right format specifier: 7 / 2, 7 % 2, 7.0 / 2, (float)7 / 2, (float)(7 / 2), -7 / 2, -7 % 2.
steps: Write your predictions first.
Run it.
The two cast lines give different answers. Write down why.
exercises.done: You got at least six of seven, or understand every miss.

exercises.title: = vs == and the missing &
exercises.what: Two classic beginner bugs, done on purpose so you recognise them later.
steps: Change an == in an if to =. Build with /W4 and read the warning. What does the program do now?
Remove the & from a scanf. Build, run, type a number. What happens?
Fix both, and write one line on why each one went wrong.
exercises.done: You've seen both failures with your own eyes and written down the symptom.

exercises.title: A menu that loops
exercises.what: Write a calculator menu: 1 add, 2 subtract, 3 multiply, 4 quit. Use do { } while and switch.
steps: Each option reads two numbers and prints the result.
Typing 7 prints 'not an option' and shows the menu again.
Quit only on 4.
exercises.done: You can't crash it or escape the loop by typing a wrong number.

exercises.title: Three loops, one problem
exercises.what: Print the numbers 1–30, but 'Fizz' for multiples of 3, 'Buzz' for 5 and 'FizzBuzz' for both.
steps: Write it with a for loop.
Rewrite it with while.
Rewrite it counting down from 30 with do { } while.
exercises.done: All three versions print the same lines (the third in reverse).

exercises.title: Why srand goes outside the loop
exercises.what: Move srand(time(NULL)) inside a loop that prints five rand() % 100 values.
steps: Run it and look at the five numbers.
Move it back outside and run again.
Write two sentences explaining the difference.
exercises.done: Your note explains what a seed is without using the word 'random'.

exercises.title: High-score insert from memory
exercises.what: Rebuild just the part of the high-score table that inserts a new score and pushes the rest down.
steps: Start from int scores[MAX_SCORES] already sorted.
Insert 3 test scores: one at the top, one in the middle, one too low to make it.
Print the table after each insert.
exercises.done: All three cases print correctly and nothing falls off the wrong end.

exercises.title: sizeof in main vs in a function
exercises.what: Print sizeof(a) / sizeof(a[0]) for a 10-int array in main, then inside a function that receives the array.
steps: Predict both numbers before running.
Run it. They won't match.
Write down your best guess why. Phase 3.5 explains it, so check your guess then.
exercises.done: You know why every array function also takes a count.

exercises.title: A string with no end
exercises.what: Make char s[3] = {'a','b','c'}; and print it with %s.
steps: Predict what prints.
Run it a few times. Note what comes after 'abc'.
Fix it two ways: make room for '\0', or use a string literal.
exercises.done: You can explain why printf kept going.

exercises.title: min, max and average functions
exercises.what: Write three small functions that each take (int arr[], int count).
steps: min and max return an int, average returns a float.
Test with three arrays, including one with a single element.
Check the average of {1, 2} prints 1.5, not 1.
exercises.done: All three work on all three arrays, with prototypes at the top of the file.

exercises.title: What strcmp returns
exercises.what: Write four strcmp calls: equal strings, 'apple' vs 'banana', 'banana' vs 'apple', 'Apple' vs 'apple'.
steps: Predict negative, zero or positive for each.
Run it.
Explain the uppercase one.
exercises.done: You'd never write if (strcmp(a, b)) to mean 'equal' again.

exercises.title: Save and load five scores
exercises.what: Write the scores array to scores.txt with fprintf, then read it back with fscanf in a fresh run.
steps: Save, close the program, run again, load, print.
Delete scores.txt and run again.
Handle fopen returning NULL with a friendly message instead of a crash.
exercises.done: It survives a missing file.

exercises.title: Pointer trace sheet
exercises.what: int x = 5; int *p = &x; *p = 10; int y = *p + 1;
steps: On paper, draw x, y and p as boxes and track every value line by line.
Print x, y, *p, and whether p == &x.
Add p = &y; *p = 0; and predict again.
exercises.done: Your paper boxes match the output.

exercises.title: swap(), the right way
exercises.what: Write swap(int a, int b) first and show it does nothing. Then write swap(int *a, int *b) that works.
steps: Print the values before and after each version.
Use the working one to sort three numbers smallest first.
Comment why the first version failed.
exercises.done: Three numbers come out sorted using only your swap.

exercises.title: The damage that didn't land
exercises.what: Write void damage(Player p, int amount) that subtracts health. Call it and print health afterwards.
steps: Predict the health after the call.
Set a breakpoint (F9) inside damage, step with F10, and watch p change while the original doesn't.
Fix it with Player *p and p->health.
exercises.done: You watched the copy change in the debugger.

exercises.title: Crash on purpose, under the debugger
exercises.what: Set a pointer to NULL and read through it. Run with F5, not from the terminal.
steps: See where the debugger stops and what it says.
Add the check that prevents it.
Write down the error text so you'll recognise it next time.
exercises.done: You know what a NULL crash looks like in Visual Studio.

exercises.title: Enemy list with an enum
exercises.what: Make an Enemy struct with health and an enum type (SLIME, BAT, SKELETON). Store five in an array.
steps: Write print_alive(const Enemy *list, int count).
Damage two by index until one dies.
Print a type name with a switch on the enum.
exercises.done: Only living enemies print, with their type names.

exercises.title: Make the linker complain
exercises.what: Split a function into a .h and a .c. Then break it.
steps: Declare it in the .h but leave the .c out of build.bat. Read LNK2019.
Put it back. Remove #pragma once and include the header twice. Read that error.
Write one line on compiler errors vs linker errors.
exercises.done: You can tell from the error code whether it's the compiler or the linker.

exercises.title: Two-clone merge conflict
exercises.what: Clone your exercises repo twice. Edit the same line in both, push from one, pull in the other.
steps: Read the conflict markers before touching anything.
Resolve by keeping parts of both.
Commit, push, and pull in the first clone to confirm they match.
exercises.done: Both clones show the same log and the same file.

exercises.title: One full branch round trip
exercises.what: Do the whole flow on one tiny change: branch, two commits, push, pull request, merge, delete, pull main.
steps: git switch -c a branch with a clear name.
Open the PR on GitHub and read your own diff before merging.
Back on main, git pull and git branch -d.
exercises.done: git log --oneline on main shows the merge.

exercises.title: Build junk in git status
exercises.what: Build something and run git status. See the .exe and .obj files waiting.
steps: Add a .gitignore and watch them disappear.
Commit an .exe on purpose in a test repo, then add it to .gitignore. Does it go away?
Fix it with git rm --cached.
exercises.done: You know .gitignore only stops new files.

exercises.title: Rewrite your worst commit messages
exercises.what: Run git log --oneline on your exercises repo.
steps: Pick the three least useful messages.
In a note, rewrite each one so a stranger would know what changed and why.
Don't change history. This is practice for next time.
exercises.done: Your next real commit follows the pattern.

exercises.title: The game loop skeleton
exercises.what: From a blank file, write input, update, render, wait, with a counter instead of a game.
steps: _kbhit()/_getch() for input, Q to quit.
Update adds 1 each frame, render redraws it on one line with \r.
Sleep at the end.
exercises.done: The counter ticks on one line and Q quits instantly.

exercises.title: Mess with the frame
exercises.what: Change the runner's timing and watch what breaks.
steps: Remove fflush(stdout). What changes on screen?
Try Sleep(16), Sleep(100) and no Sleep at all.
Write down why the game speed changes with the frame rate. Phase 6 fixes this with dt.
exercises.done: You can explain why 'move 1 per frame' isn't a speed.

exercises.title: Forget the -1
exercises.what: Comment out the line that resets an obstacle slot to -1 after it passes.
steps: Predict what you'll see after a few seconds.
Run it.
Put it back and write one line on what a sentinel value is for.
exercises.done: Your prediction was right, or you know why it wasn't.

exercises.title: Add a PAUSED state
exercises.what: Draw the runner's state machine on paper, then add PAUSED.
steps: P pauses during PLAYING, P again resumes.
Nothing moves and the score doesn't change while paused.
Show 'PAUSED' on screen.
exercises.done: You added a state without touching the other states' code.

exercises.title: One new mechanic
exercises.what: Add one thing to the runner: a pickup that adds 10 points, a second lane, or a speed-up every 100 points.
steps: Decide which state and which function it belongs in before you write code.
Keep it to one commit.
Play it for two minutes. Is it more fun?
exercises.done: It's committed with a message that says what and why.

exercises.title: Blank window from memory
exercises.what: Write WinMain, register the class, create the window and run the message loop from a blank file.
steps: You get one lookup. Note what you needed it for.
Build with user32.lib.
Closing the window ends the program.
exercises.done: A window opens and closes cleanly.

exercises.title: Comment the message loop
exercises.what: Add a comment to every line of your message loop and WndProc.
steps: Explain GetMessage vs PeekMessage in two lines each.
Explain why a game uses PeekMessage.
Say which line runs when you press a key.
exercises.done: You could draw the path of a key press from the keyboard to your code.

exercises.title: Remove the pieces one at a time
exercises.what: Break the moving rectangle in two ways.
steps: Remove InvalidateRect. The rectangle's position changes but the screen doesn't. Why?
Put it back. Drop gdi32.lib from build.bat and read the linker error.
Fix both.
exercises.done: You know which errors come from the build and which only show on screen.

exercises.title: Two rectangles, two keysets
exercises.what: Add a second rectangle moved with WASD while the first uses the arrow keys.
steps: Store both in structs, not loose variables.
Change a rectangle's colour when you press space.
Keep both inside the window.
exercises.done: Both move at the same time without interfering.

exercises.title: Measure your frame time
exercises.what: Print the frame time with QueryPerformanceCounter.
steps: Predict the number with no Sleep, then with Sleep(16).
Run both and compare.
Write down why Sleep(16) isn't exactly 16 ms.
exercises.done: You've seen real frame times, not guessed ones.

exercises.title: AABB on paper first
exercises.what: Write four pairs of rectangles as x, y, w, h: one overlapping, one touching edges, one apart, one inside the other.
steps: Decide on paper which ones collide.
Run them through your AABB function.
Decide what 'touching' should count as in your game, and make the code agree.
exercises.done: Your function and your paper agree on all four.

exercises.title: Speed that depends on frame rate
exercises.what: Move the player a fixed number of pixels per frame. Cap at 30 fps, then 60.
steps: Watch how fast it moves at each cap.
Change it to speed * dt.
Run both caps again. The speed should match.
exercises.done: Movement looks the same speed at 30 and 60 fps.

exercises.title: The state switch from memory
exercises.what: In a fresh file, write MENU → PLAYING → GAME_OVER with an enum, a switch and next_state.
steps: Each state draws one line of text.
Enter moves forward, R from GAME_OVER restarts.
Compare with the prototype's version.
exercises.done: State changes only happen in one place.

exercises.title: One item off the stretch list
exercises.what: Pick one: a moving enemy, the score drawn on screen, or a best score that survives a restart.
steps: Write in a note where it hooks in: input, update or render.
Build it in one branch.
Play it and write one line on whether it made the game better.
exercises.done: It's merged and you played it.

exercises.title: Read code you didn't write
exercises.what: Pick one function in the prototype that Person A wrote, or one you got from Claude.
steps: Add a comment above every few lines explaining what they do.
Mark any line you can't explain with // ?.
Look those up, or bring them to your next sync.
exercises.done: No // ? left, or you know who to ask.

exercises.title: Prompt it back
exercises.what: Pick a function you wrote last week. Write a prompt that should make Claude Code produce the same function.
steps: Name the function, parameters, return type and constraints.
Run it in a scratch folder and diff against yours.
Every difference is a detail your prompt left out. Rewrite it once.
exercises.done: The second prompt gets much closer than the first.

exercises.title: Read every line before you run it
exercises.what: Ask Claude for something small, like clamp(int v, int lo, int hi) or a function that wraps an index around an array.
steps: Before running it, comment every line.
Find one thing to simplify and ask for it.
Then run it with three test values.
exercises.done: You didn't run any line you couldn't explain.

exercises.title: Explain it back to Claude
exercises.what: Ask Claude to explain a piece of your own code. Then close the reply.
steps: Write your own explanation from memory.
Paste it back and ask Claude what you got wrong or left out.
Save the correction as a task note.
exercises.done: Your explanation holds up.
